Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-14
Start time (UTC): 15:00
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Tom Reilly (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (Acme CTO), Priya Rao (Acme ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Acme Eng Mgr)

Summary (auto-gen, may be imperfect):
Quick scoping call to align on POC success criteria for a retrieval-augmented generation workload; primary focus on unit economics (per-token cost), batching/caching knobs, and defining benchmarks and timeline for a 3-4 week pilot. Action items and next steps captured at end.

Topics:
- Workload sizing: qps, avg tokens/request, peak patterns
- Success criteria: latency SLOs, cost per 1M tokens, quality/regression thresholds
- Benchmarks: what to run (hosted vs dedicated), metrics to capture
- Timeline and procurement constraints

Transcript:
[00:00] Tom (Redwood-AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — I'm Tom, AE on the account, and with me is Maya from our SE team.
[00:07] Maya (Redwood-SE): Hey all. we'll focus on the cost modeling and how we size the POC. please tell us the workload and constraints.
[00:12] Carlos (Acme-CTO): yeah thanks. Carlos here. we're exploring using LLMs for customer support summarization and some classification. we have a few constraints: budget cap for the quarter, and latency needs — p95 under 250ms ideally.
[00:22] Priya (Acme-ML): For the ML specifics, average payload is around 600 tokens outgoing, we do about 20 rps steady state, peaks up to 120 rps for short periods. most calls are small though, median is ~180 tokens.
[00:34] Liam (Acme-Eng): want to make sure we can push into a dedicated setup if needed for cost predictability. procurement lead time is about 4 weeks.
[00:42] Tom: Great, that helps. Maya, do you want to walk through the simple per-token model and the knobs?
[00:46] Maya: Sure — so, at a high level we model cost as tokens * unit_price + infra. unit_price varies by model and deployment mode. hosted is pay-as-you-go with slightly higher unit token costs; dedicated is a reserved capacity where the marginal per-token cost can be lower after you amortize the committed monthly spend. Also, caching and batching drastically change unit economics.
[01:10] Carlos: can you give ballpark numbers? our finance wants to know per 1M tokens what to expect.
[01:15] Maya: ballpark, using an open LLM variant we often see hosted token costs equivalent to about $7–$20 per 1M tokens depending on model size and whether it's generation or embeddings. dedicated can drop that to $2–$8 per 1M tokens once you amortize. these are rough — we'll send a spreadsheet.
[01:35] Priya: that's a wide range; where does batching enter?
[01:38] Maya: batching increases throughput and reduces per-token compute overhead. example: with small requests (50–200 tokens), batching at the runtime can get you 2–3x better cost efficiency, but it adds latency risk. continuous batching with latency SLOs can still maintain p95 targets if you configure max-delay and smart routing.
[02:00] Tom: also our KV cache and prefix caching are big factors. if you have a lot of repeated prefixes or conversation context, cache hit rate can cut generation compute by 30–60%. but note transcription sometimes calls it K V cash or KV cash, people get confused in notes.
[02:14] Carlos: can you run the numbers for our case: avg 600 tokens, 20 rps steady, peaks 120 rps — and let's assume 40% of requests are repeated templates (cacheable).
[02:25] Maya: rough calc on the fly: 20 rps * 600 tokens * 3600 sec = that's large, hold on — we should convert to tokens per day. 20 rps steady --> 20 * 3600 * 24? oh sorry math slip: 20 rps * 3600 = 72k tokens per hour times 24 = 1.728M requests? Actually I'm mixing. let's do tokens: 20 req/s * 600 tokens = 12k tokens/s. per hour = 43.2M tokens; per day = 1.0368B tokens. with 40% cache hit assume effective tokens generated = 0.6 * 1.0368B = ~622M tokens/day.
[03:04] Priya: that seems high — maybe I misstated rps, our 20 was concurrent users not requests per second. sorry, it's more like 2 rps average per user, total steady requests maybe 40rps — hmm i need to confirm.
[03:18] Liam: yeah we'll provide exact traffic trace. good call.
[03:22] Maya: ok that matters, please share the 7-day trace — that will let us run an accurate benchmark.
[03:27] Tom: on benchmarks, we usually run both hosted and a small dedicated pool. Maya, what's a realistic dedicated sizing for this workload?
[03:33] Maya: depends on model choice and quantization. for a 7B-ish model quantized to 4-bit running on A100/4, a small pool of 4-8 GPUs can handle tens to low hundreds of rps depending on batching. but if you go with bigger context lengths or 70B models numbers change. For the POC we recommend starting small: 2-GPU dedicated pool + a hosted fallback. That lets us measure latency and unit cost with a representative workload.
[03:55] Carlos: procurement beware — if dedicated requires a 3-month commit that's a blocker. can we do a trial?
[04:00] Tom: we have flexible trial options for POCs; sometimes we do a time-limited dedicated evaluation or use burstable capacity. we'll document options.
[04:08] Priya: what metrics should we measure in the benchmark?
[04:11] Maya: p95 latency, cold-start token latency, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, batching efficiency (avg batch size, wait time), KV cache hit rate, error rate, and per-token cost computed as total infra cost / generated tokens. Also qualitative metrics: output quality, hallucination rate on our eval prompts.
[04:29] Tom: and we'll instrument per-route cost breakdowns in the console so you can see token, compute, and infra components.
[04:35] Carlos: about caching — if 40% is cacheable, what's the impact on infra cost?
[04:40] Maya: assume cache hit avoids model forward pass entirely for the prefix portion; in practice effective compute reduction will be 20–50% depending on cache hit semantics and how much of the sequence is cached. So your per-token cost could drop by similar fraction. We'll simulate that in the spreadsheet.
[04:59] Priya: for batching knobs — what's your recommendation for our latency SLO 250ms?
[05:03] Maya: use continuous batching with max latency 25–40ms wait per token and conservative max batch size. also route low-latency traffic to a hot pool and bulk/async traffic to a cost-optimized pool. that gives a balance of latency and cost.
[05:15] Carlos: ok what about quantization impact on quality vs cost?
[05:18] Maya: quantization to 4-bit often gives 1.5–3x cost throughput improvement with small quality delta for many tasks; but it depends on model and your prompts. part of the POC is to A/B quantized vs fp16 to measure regressions. we'll include prompt-sets from Priya for that.
[05:34] Liam: timeline: we need a POC that shows clear numbers in about 3 weeks. procurement takes 4 weeks, but we can run the POC in parallel. is 3 weeks realistic?
[05:43] Tom: yes, typical POC cadence: week 0 collect data & instrumentation + setup; week 1 run benchmarks; week 2 iterate on knobs (batching/caching/quant), week 3 collect final metrics and cost report. so ~3-4 weeks.
[05:57] Carlos: success criteria for us — p95 latency <250ms in 95% of traffic, cost per 1M tokens < $X (we'll confirm X with finance), and no major regressions in quality.
[06:09] Maya: noted. we'll propose tentative thresholds in the spreadsheet but you should fill in the finance target.
[06:15] Tom: any security blockers? private deployment or VPC needed?
[06:18] Carlos: initially we're fine with hosted but will need VPC/private for production due to data residency. we need SOC2 and audit logs.
[06:26] Tom: we'll share SOC2 and KMS details; private deployment options discussed.
[06:29] Priya: small note: please include example of per-token calc in the spreadsheet — show explicit line items (model price, infra amortization, caching delta, batching multiplier).
[06:39] Maya: will do. we'll also include an example with 40% cache hit and varying batch sizes to show sensitivity.
[06:46] Carlos: are there any gotchas on token counting e.g., if we do retrieval-augmented generation and add 1k tokens of context?
[06:52] Maya: yes retrieval context increases tokens in both prompt and KV usage. we treat retriever tokens as input tokens for cost. prefix caching can help if same docs are reused. also we support reranking/embedding offload to cheaper endpoints.
[07:05] Liam: ok for benchmarks we want hosted vs dedicated numbers and also a mixed routing scenario with fallback.
[07:12] Tom: agreed. action items recap in just a sec. Maya, anything else on knobs?
[07:17] Maya: just to call out smart routing: you can route by latency sensitivity and by cost. e.g., high-value requests go to dedicated low-latency pool, bulk processing goes to cost-optimized hosted or lower-precision models.
[07:28] Carlos: competitor question: do you support smooth fallbacks if a model from vendor X is cheaper? we've heard some folks use Anthropic or OpenAI as a fallback.
[07:36] Tom: yes we can route to different model providers or model variants; we call that multi-tier routing. will include examples.
[07:42] Priya: ok next steps?
[07:44] Tom: I'll send the cost-model spreadsheet and a proposed POC plan. Maya will spin up benchmarks and share scripts. Priya/Carlos will provide traffic trace and prompt set. we'll tentatively target pilot kickoff week of 2025-03-03.
[07:57] Carlos: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[08:00] Tom: thanks all, we'll follow up via email.
